paragraphs.text: A popular song asks the question: 'Who made the doughnut with the hole in the middle?' The answer can be somewhat complex. Although the concept of fried dough is not limited to one country or culture, the origin of the modern American doughnut is generally traced back to a treat brought to New York by the Dutch. Called the 'oily cake', these fried pastries did not yet have the famous ring form but were otherwise similar to modern doughnuts.

Not much more is known about the doughnut until the mid-19th century, when a ship captain's mother named Elizabeth Gregory made a deep-fried dough that used spice from her son's cargo of nutmeg and cinnamon, along with lemon rind. She made the dough so her son and his crew could store it on long voyages, hoping it might help prevent severe vitamin deficiency and colds. Mrs Gregory put hazelnuts or walnuts in the center, where the dough might not cook through, and then called them doughnuts.

However, it is Elizabeth Gregory's son who is credited with putting the hole in the doughnut. Some doughnut historians maintain that Captain Gregory did it to save on ingredients. Others say that he gave the doughnut its shape when, needing to keep both hands on the wheel in a storm, he skewered one of his mom's doughnuts on a spoke of his ship's wheel. In an interview with the Boston Post at the turn of the century, Captain Gregory tried to stop such rumors with his recollection of the moment 50 years before: he said he had used the top of a round tin pepper box and cut into the middle of a doughnut the first doughnut hole ever seen by mortal eyes.'

It wasn't, though, until World War I (1914-1918) that doughnuts became popular. Millions of homesick American soldiers called 'doughboys' ate doughnuts while stationed in France. They were served up by women volunteers who brought them to the front lines to give soldiers a taste of home. One of these volunteers used the top of a coffee pot to create the ideal ring shape. When the doughboys came back from the war, they had a natural liking for more doughnuts. The name 'doughboy', however, goes back earlier to the American Civil War (1861-1865), when foot soldiers were called doughboys, perhaps because their brass buttons resembled flour dumplings.

The first doughnut machine did not appear until 1920, in New York City, when Adolph Levitt, an enterprising refugee from Russia, began selling fried doughnuts from his bakery. Hungry theater crowds expressed their desire for some way to turn out the doughnuts faster, and Levitt took on the challenge.

Levitt's doughnut machine turned the production of doughnuts into a kind of public entertainment. Since then, generations of children have delighted in the scene behind the glass of doughnut shops and have learned some secrets in the process - for example, the fact that the dough is dropped into the hot oil already with its final doughnut shape, and does not need to be cut out.

The machines grew more refined, and the idea spread. By the 1930s, Adolph Levitt's machines were earning him $25 million a year, mostly from deliveries all over the US. One article noted that the doughnut machine had diminished the prejudice that had been directed at the 'grease-soaked product' by making it into a light, puffy product of a machine.'

By the 1934 World's Fair in Chicago, doughnuts were billed as 'the food hit of the Century of Progress.' A doughnut cost less than five cents, within reach of the era's countless poor. Occasionally, the treats were served with messages to lift the spirits: 'As you go through life make this your goal: Watch the doughnut, not the hole.'

It was in the 1930s, too, that the Frenchman Joe LeBeau traveled from Louisiana to Kentucky to sell his secret recipe, along with the brand name Krispy Kreme, to a local store owner who then hired his own nephew Vernon Rudolph and put him to work selling the treats to local homes. A few years later, Rudolph founded his own Krispy Kreme enterprise in North Carolina. There he was successful as a wholesale doughnut supplier but added to his earnings by selling doughnuts to passers-by as well.

Doughnuts were as popular in World War II (1939-1945) as they had been at any other time. Volunteer nurses, later known as 'Doughnut Dollies', passed them out. The famous composer Irving Berlin romanticized the doughnut even further in his 1942 army musical that revolves around a soldier who falls in love while eating doughnuts.

By the late 1950s, there were Krispy Kreme doughnut outlets in 12 states, and a new Massachusetts company called Dunkin' Donuts had been going strong since it was founded in 1950. Smaller companies like one called Ring King Jr were driven out of business because they couldn't compete with the efficiency of the large chains. For a while in New York City, the popularity of the doughnut seemed to be going into decline. This was mostly due to being challenged by the bagel, a boiled bread of similar shape and size to a doughnut, which some thought of as a more sophisticated treat. But college students and others throughout the country never lost enthusiasm for the doughnut.

Today, the doughnut is thriving. In the US alone, about 10 billion doughnuts are made every year, and American doughnut chains do well in at least 37 countries outside the US. It's not surprising, then, that one continues to hear pop songs about doughnuts, or see reprints of the famous children's book Homer Price which features a doughnut-making machine which has gone crazy.
